clue.text: Ordinary, mundane job essentially lacking in colour

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its centre, so lacking it means the middle letter goes

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for ordinary
a mundane job is a CHORE; its central O is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone doing a dull, ordinary task that has no colour to it.
explanation.walkthrough: CHORE has five letters, so its essential middle letter is the O; remove it and put the ordinary O in front to get OCHRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is an earthy yellow-brown pigment and the shade named after it.

clue.text: Miserable people scrounged off accommodating Greek character

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room to, so one group of letters houses another
something off has gone wrong or bad, so these letters are out of their proper order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: Grumpy people who cadged things from a Greek person they put up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like part of the phrase 'scrounged off', but it is the signal to rearrange; the Greek letter lands inside the rearranged word.
explanation.definitionFit: Curmudgeons are bad-tempered, grumbling old people, so a fair description of miserable folk.

clue.text: Rustic American protected by upstanding state bureaucrat

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means reading from bottom to top
something protected is held inside other things, so the letters sit within the following words

parts.note: the letters straddling the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A country bumpkin in the US shielded by an honest official of the state.
explanation.walkthrough: Read up through the end of 'state' and the start of 'bureaucrat' to find RUBE.
explanation.definitionFit: Rube is American slang for an unsophisticated country person, a hick or yokel.

clue.text: Are their bananas more nutritious?

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, and crazy letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wondering whether a certain group's bananas are better for you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like the fruit being asked about, but it is slang for mad and signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A hearty meal is substantial and nourishing, so heartier food is more filling and sustaining.

clue.text: And everything else about this place is otherworldly

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: et al, Latin shorthand for 'and others'
here means this place

explanation.surface: A claim that everything about this spot seems unearthly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And everything else' is the Latin et al, which splits in two to hold the place word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethereal describes something delicate and heavenly, seemingly too light and spiritual for this world.

clue.text: Appeased Unionist leaves assembly in rush

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a rush is a reed-like marsh plant

indicators.note: someone who leaves departs, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for Unionist, the letter removed
an assembly is a COUNCIL, which loses its U

explanation.surface: A placated Northern Irish Unionist walks out of a meeting in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rush' reads as haste but is the plant; COUNCIL minus U goes inside REED. Unionists are a Northern Irish political tradition.
explanation.definitionFit: To be reconciled is to be brought to accept or be pacified, much like being appeased.

clue.text: Evil bishop redacted from account

indicators.note: redacted text is blacked out of a document, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a bill is an account of money owed
B is the chess notation for bishop, the letter taken out

explanation.surface: A wicked churchman whose name has been blacked out of a report.
explanation.walkthrough: BILL without its B leaves ILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill can mean harmful or wicked, as in ill deeds or ill will, a sense matching evil.

clue.text: Resume abandoned party in lodge

indicators.note: work that is abandoned is left unfinished, so only the start of the word survives

parts.note: the word truncated, dropping its last four letters to keep its first two
a side is a party in a dispute or contest

explanation.surface: A CV left behind at a party held in a lodge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resume' tempts as the verb 'carry on', but it is only raw material to be cut short; 'lodge' is a verb, not the building.
explanation.definitionFit: To lodge somewhere is to live there as a tenant or guest, so it means to dwell or stay.

clue.text: Artist runs into elegant youths; they are quintessentially straight

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, the crosswords' usual artist

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so one letter is placed inside another piece

parts.note: mods were sharply dressed 1960s British youths
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A painter charges into a group of stylish young people who are all very proper.
explanation.walkthrough: Mods were a smartly suited British youth subculture of the 1960s. 'straight' in the surface means honest; in the definition it means unbent.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'straight as a ramrod' makes these gun-cleaning rods the proverbial image of perfect straightness.

clue.text: Swimmer wildly exaggerated finale of race on river

parts.note: OTT, over the top, means wildly exaggerated

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of race
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A swimmer makes too much of the dramatic end of a river race.
explanation.walkthrough: OTT (over the top) is a common British abbreviation for excessive or exaggerated.
explanation.definitionFit: The otter is an aquatic mammal that spends much of its life swimming in rivers.

clue.text: Circus entertainer regularly exhibiting a score of beasts

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is put on show

parts.note: the first, third, fifth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A circus performer who routinely shows off twenty animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'score' looks like the number twenty, but it only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrobats perform tumbling and trapeze feats and are a traditional circus act.

clue.text: Ne'er-do-well exposed following closure of British barracks

indicators.note: exposed means stripped of its covering, so the outside letters come off
one piece following another is placed after it in the answer
a closure is an ending, so only the last letter is taken

parts.note: the last letter of British
a ne'er-do-well is FECKLESS; lose its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A good-for-nothing is caught out after a British military base is shut down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barracks' looks like a noun, the soldiers' quarters, but it is the verb meaning to jeer. Feckless is used as a noun here, a feckless person.
explanation.definitionFit: To barrack a speaker, in British usage, is to shout them down with jeers, just as a heckler does.

clue.text: Nonsense about United's humiliating defeat

indicators.note: to be about something is to go around it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: rot is nonsense
U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names

explanation.surface: Pundits talking rubbish about a football team's thrashing.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as 'is': the wordplay is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rout is a crushing, disorderly defeat in which the loser is overwhelmed.

clue.text: Remember Marine shot in twenty-nine

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: 29-down's answer is TIE, and bind is a synonym for tie

indicators.note: something shot is ruined or wrecked, so its letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Commemorate a marine who was shot in 1929.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twenty-nine' looks like a year or age, but it is a cross-reference to the clue numbered 29, whose answer TIE has the synonym needed here.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear something in mind is to keep it in your memory, an idiom for remembering.

clue.text: Ruthlessly incorporated elderly relatives

parts.note: Inc. is the standard abbreviation for incorporated, as after US company names
elderly means old
blood means kin, as in 'blood is thicker than water'

explanation.surface: Old family members were heartlessly absorbed into a company.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay's pieces straddle the answer's word breaks, so the enumeration 2,4,5 hides how it is built.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in cold blood means doing something deliberately and without pity, the essence of ruthlessness.

clue.text: Eccentric grandee touring Spain with extremely talkative deviant

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all round it, so one piece surrounds another
an eccentric is off-centre and odd, so the letters are set out of their usual order

parts.note: taken as written
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: An odd Spanish nobleman travels around Spain with a chatty reprobate.
explanation.walkthrough: E for Spain comes from international car registration plates. Only the grandee and Spain letters are rearranged; the talkative ends stay put at the finish.
explanation.definitionFit: A degenerate is a person whose morals have sunk low, someone whose behaviour strays from accepted norms.

clue.text: Resolute female, having captured two Germans, died

indicators.note: a captor holds prisoners inside, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a doe is a female deer or rabbit
G is the abbreviation for German, twice
d. is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: A determined woman took two German prisoners before she died.
explanation.walkthrough: 'female' suggests a woman, but crosswords often use it for a female animal, here a deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogged describes tenacious, stubborn persistence, the quality of someone who is resolute.

clue.text: Fanatics from Northern Ireland initially admitted hacking computers

indicators.note: hacking into a system means getting inside it, so these letters break into another piece

parts.note: Macs are Apple computers

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of admitted
NI is the abbreviation for Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Extremists from Northern Ireland confessed at first to breaking into computers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' links definition and wordplay; 'computers' is the brand name of Apple machines, plural.
explanation.definitionFit: A maniac, in the loose sense, is an obsessive enthusiast, much like a fanatic or zealot.

clue.text: Put one's foot down over energy charge

parts.note: to put your foot down forcefully is to stamp; past tense
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone taking a firm stand about the price of their power bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put one's foot down' suggests being firm, but here it is literal: stamped. In a down clue 'over' puts STAMPED above E. 'charge' looks like a fee but is a rush.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden headlong rush of a panicking crowd or herd, a wild charge.

clue.text: Sugar daddy's first to forsake Scandinavian ex, say?

indicators.note: to forsake is to abandon, so the named initial letter is dropped

parts.note: a Swede is a Scandinavian; without D it is SWEE
the first letter of daddy, the one that goes
ex is the letter X, which as a Roman numeral is ten; 'say' flags the example

explanation.surface: A wealthy older lover is told to drop his Scandinavian former partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sugar daddy' looks like one phrase, but Sugar is the definition, a verb here. 'ex' is the name of the letter X, the Roman ten.
explanation.definitionFit: To sugar a drink or dish is to add sweetness to it, which is exactly to sweeten.

clue.text: Trust article on European food

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another comes after it, so the earlier words are placed second

parts.note: a Pole is a European from Poland
NT is the National Trust, the British heritage charity
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A trust places an article about European cuisine.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust looks after historic British houses and land, hence its NT abbreviation in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Polenta is an Italian dish of boiled cornmeal, a staple food of northern Italy.

clue.text: Echo fills empty brothel with deep, booming sound

indicators.note: to fill something is to go inside it, so one letter is placed within another piece
an empty word has had its contents removed, so only its outer letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of brothel
Echo is the NATO alphabet word for E
a deep voice is low

explanation.surface: Deep, reverberating sounds echo through a deserted brothel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Echo' looks like the reverberation, but it is the radio code word for its letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A bellow is a loud, deep roar like that of a bull, a resonant booming noise.

clue.text: Decorate Bond's superior sounding superior

indicators.note: sounding means as heard, so we write down how the letter is pronounced

parts.note: M is James Bond's boss in the spy novels, spoken as the letter's name
a boss is a superior at work

explanation.surface: Pinning a medal on James Bond's senior officer.
explanation.walkthrough: M, the head of MI6 in the Bond stories, is written out as the letter's spoken name EM.
explanation.definitionFit: To emboss is to ornament a surface with a raised design, a way of decorating it.

clue.text: Knight stops looting for a quick bite

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a hole, so one letter is lodged inside another piece

parts.note: to sack a town is to plunder it
N is the chess notation for knight

explanation.surface: A knight halts a pillage to grab something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: In chess notation K is the king, so the knight is N; it goes inside SACK.
explanation.definitionFit: A snack is a small, hurried meal eaten between main meals, just a quick bite.

clue.text: Brains behind putting curbs on motorway in Maryland

parts.note: to master an urge is to curb it
M, as in M1, is the British motorway prefix
taken as written
the D of MD, Maryland's abbreviation, whose M the motorway has already supplied

explanation.surface: The planner behind imposing traffic limits on a Maryland highway.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is loose: it wants IN placed inside Maryland's MD, with the motorway's M doubling as MD's M. Read 'Brains behind' together as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The mastermind is the person who plans and directs a scheme, the brains behind it.

clue.text: Discovered android with electronic instrument

indicators.note: dis-covered means with its cover taken off, so the outer letters are removed

parts.note: an android is a ROBOT; strip its first and last letters
E is the abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail

explanation.surface: Someone found a robot that plays a synthesiser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' reads as 'found', but split as dis-covered it means uncovered: ROBOT loses its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The oboe is a double-reed woodwind instrument used in orchestras.

clue.text: Pretentious type has no business taking part

indicators.note: to take part is to take a portion, so the letters come from part of the words

parts.note: the letters across the ends of the three words

explanation.surface: A snooty person has no right to be joining in.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts with the S at the end of 'has' and ends at the B of 'business'.
explanation.definitionFit: A snob looks down on others and affects superior taste, the classic pretentious sort.

clue.text: Open University stirred up great indignation

parts.note: OU is the Open University, Britain's distance-learning university

indicators.note: things stirred up are mixed around, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A university provokes a storm of anger among the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'great' seems to go with indignation, but it is the fodder to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Outrage is a strong feeling of anger and shock at something unjust, a synonym for indignation.

clue.text: Link that is attached to end of text

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the last letter of text
i.e. is the Latin abbreviation for 'that is'

explanation.surface: A hyperlink placed at the end of a written message.
explanation.walkthrough: IE is attached to T, which is placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie is something that binds or connects, so a link or bond between two things.

clue.text: Prisoner put on parole ultimately gets pardon

parts.note: a con is a convict
to don clothes is to put them on

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of parole

explanation.surface: An inmate released on parole ends up being pardoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' reads as 'placed on', but it is DON, to dress in.
explanation.definitionFit: To condone is to overlook or forgive an offence, much as to pardon excuses it.

clue.text: Ran through gardens in Home Counties visibly embarrassed

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: the Home Counties surround London in south-east England, SE
Kew Gardens are the Royal Botanic Gardens in London
an embarrassed person goes red

explanation.surface: Someone red-faced after dashing through gardens outside London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran through' looks like jogging, but it means stabbing. The Home Counties are the counties around London, in England's south-east.
explanation.definitionFit: To run someone through is to pierce them with a sword, which is to skewer them.

clue.text: Several feet behind sailor's quarters

indicators.note: one thing behind another comes after it, so that piece is placed second

parts.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman
an ode is a poem, made of several metrical feet

explanation.surface: A seaman's lodgings some distance behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feet' suggests measurement, but here they are the rhythmic units of verse, so several make a poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Quarters are living accommodation, and an abode is the place where someone lives.
